name: Venus Flytrap
summary: The Venus flytrap is the accepted species Dionaea muscipula, a clumping perennial carnivore native to coastal North Carolina and a small area of northeastern South Carolina. Its hinged traps close after two trigger hairs are disturbed; use low-mineral water and keep the acidic medium wet, without fertilizer.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Dionaea muscipula J.Ellis and places it in Droseraceae. The common name Venus flytrap refers to this species here; no named cultivar is implied.

growth.short: Low rosette of hinged traps; trap closure is normal prey response
growth.guidance: NC State describes a basal rosette of up to eight leaves. Each leaf ends in a two-lobed trap; disturbance of any two of six trigger hairs can close it, and the trap resets after digestion. Trap interiors may be green or red depending on sun exposure. This species description does not assign a cultivar or trap color.

cultivation.short: Keep the acidic, sandy medium wet and use rain or distilled water
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends high humidity, wet sandy acidic medium, and full sun to partial shade; it says not to let the medium dry. It recommends rainwater or distilled water because hard or treated water can harm the plant, and says not to fertilize. Container/bog use is documented, but this is not evidence for recirculating hydroponic nutrient solution.

propagation.guidance: North Carolina Extension lists seed and division as propagation strategies. The source does not specify a home seed-sowing protocol, germination timing, or cultivar fidelity; those details remain unresolved.

flowering.short: White flowers rise on a leafless stalk in spring
flowering.guidance: NC State describes clusters of small white flowers on a leafless stalk in May and June in its regional North Carolina context. Flowering is part of the species lifecycle; no indoor calendar is inferred.

problems.short: Watch for aphids, spider mites and black spot
problems.guidance: NC State reports no serious insect or disease problems but lists aphids, spider mites and black spot to watch for. It also warns that hard or treated water can harm the plant and identifies the species as endangered, advising against wild collection. Choose nursery-propagated stock; these are source-region conservation notes and monitoring cues, not a diagnosis from trap appearance alone.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Wetland ecology does not establish suitability for recirculating hydroponic nutrient solutions.

name: Cape Sundew
summary: Cape sundew is the accepted evergreen carnivorous species Drosera capensis. SANBI describes a rhizomatous plant with sticky tentacled leaves, pink-to-mauve flowers, a continuously moist potting context and vegetative propagation; dimensions and seasonal dates remain regional source descriptions.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Drosera capensis L. and identifies its native range in the South African Cape. The public identity is species-level, not a color-form cultivar.

growth.short: Evergreen sundew with sticky tentacled leaves and pink-mauve flowers
growth.guidance: SANBI describes a robust, free-flowering evergreen perennial, usually around 15 cm high, with leaves radiating from a short rhizomatous stem. Sticky glands on the leaf tentacles trap prey; 15–30 pink-to-mauve flowers open in ascending order on a stem. SANBI's December–January flowering note is Southern Hemisphere context, not a universal calendar.

cultivation.short: Keep the pot consistently moist with low-mineral water
cultivation.guidance: SANBI's PlantZAfrica recommends a pot standing in a 1–3 cm saucer of fresh water so the medium stays moist, and full sun to semi-shade outdoors. It describes an acidic, low-nutrient medium and an indoor-facing recommendation for its South African context. This botanical-garden/container guidance is not a hydroponic nutrient recipe or a universal indoor-light tier.

propagation.short: Leaf and root cuttings are vegetative options
propagation.guidance: SANBI documents vegetative propagation from leaf or root cuttings. For the seed route and sowing instructions, use the linked Seed Profile; this Plant Profile does not repeat the seed-to-establishment protocol.

problems.short: Drying, handling and pests can change appearance
problems.guidance: SANBI notes that drying can cause drooping and reduced mucilage, while recent transplanting or touching the leaves can temporarily reduce visible dew before new foliage develops. It lists aphids, mealybugs and thrips as pests that can deform new growth and cautions against soap-based insecticides. These cues should prompt a check of conditions, not diagnosis from appearance alone.

name: Pinguicula primuliflora
summary: Pinguicula primuliflora is a compact, southeastern U.S. carnivorous perennial with sticky rosette leaves and terminal flowers. NParks documents consistently moist, sometimes waterlogged root conditions and semi-shade; the species also forms plantlets at leaf tips. These garden-botanical facts do not establish conventional hydroponic compatibility.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Pinguicula primuliflora C.E.Wood & R.K.Godfrey, in Lentibulariaceae. NParks gives Primrose Butterwort as a common name; the broader word butterwort remains a search alias, not a replacement identity.

growth.short: Compact basal rosette, typically reported 4–16 cm across
growth.guidance: NParks describes oblong, bright-green leaves in a compact basal rosette, typically 4–16 cm across, with glandular hairs that trap and digest insects. Solitary flower stalks rise from the rosette. The crown-width range is species-level botanical-garden data, not a pot or system-spacing recommendation.

cultivation.short: Keep the root zone consistently moist; semi-shade is documented
cultivation.guidance: NParks recommends a layered sphagnum/peat and sphagnum-perlite medium and says to keep it consistently moist; its record notes tolerance of moist to waterlogged root zones and semi-shade. The specialist account also describes moist, aerated medium and filtered light. Neither source supports a conventional hydroponic nutrient solution, EC/pH target, or dry-out interval.

care.short: Plantlets can develop where leaf tips touch the medium
care.guidance: NParks reports plantlets forming at leaf tips where they contact the medium; the specialist account describes them rooting before separation. This is a recognizable vegetative growth feature, not a sign of disease or a seedling protocol.

flowering.short: Solitary, terminal flowers with a pale-purple and yellow pattern
flowering.guidance: NParks describes a solitary terminal flower with a light-purple corolla and yellow throat marked by brown veins. The sources reviewed do not establish a universal indoor flowering calendar.

propagation.short: Leaf-tip plantlets are documented; reliable routine seed culture is not established here
propagation.guidance: NParks and the specialist account both describe vegetative plantlets at the leaf tips; the specialist account notes occasional seed formation in its described clone. This supports vegetative propagation but does not prove seed propagation is impossible or establish a reliable seed protocol.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Carnivorous-plant medium and waterlogging tolerance do not prove compatibility with a recirculating nutrient solution.

name: Nepenthes × ventrata
variety: Horticultural hybrid identity; no named cultivar specified
summary: Nepenthes × ventrata is a natural horticultural hybrid of N. alata and N. ventricosa with climbing stems, tendrils and pitcher traps. NParks documents moist, well-drained, low-nutrient medium and occasional misting; these houseplant/cultivation details do not establish conventional hydroponic compatibility.

identity.short: Natural hybrid identity, not a species or named cultivar claim
identity.guidance: NParks identifies Nepenthes × ventrata as a natural hybrid between N. alata and N. ventricosa. This record preserves the horticultural hybrid name and does not treat it as a named cultivar or either parent species.

growth.short: Climbing stems form tendrils and insect-trapping pitchers
growth.guidance: NParks describes glossy, leathery leaves whose tips form tendrils or cylindrical pitchers. The pitchers are yellow-green and may develop a red blush under bright light. This describes the hybrid; it is not a cultivar-specific color guarantee or a diagnosis of plant health.

cultivation.short: Moist, drained, low-nutrient medium; semi-shade is the listed care category
cultivation.guidance: NParks describes a moist but well-drained, low-nutrient medium and gives examples using perlite or sand with peat or sphagnum. Its care category lists semi-shade, while the description says 6–8 hours of full sun can develop red pitcher color. These are different contexts within the same source; no single indoor lamp target, EC or pH recipe is inferred.

care.short: Maintain humidity; NParks advises occasional misting and avoiding air-conditioned placement
care.guidance: NParks recommends maintaining a humid environment with occasional misting and avoiding an air-conditioned location. This is source-specific horticultural guidance; no exact humidity percentage or misting frequency is supplied.

propagation.short: Tissue culture is the documented commercial propagation route
propagation.guidance: NParks reports that this hybrid has been widely propagated by tissue culture. That does not establish that seed production is impossible; a reliable seed protocol and fidelity for the marketed hybrid remain unverified.

uses.short: Documented as an indoor ornamental and hanging-basket climber
uses.guidance: NParks lists Nepenthes × ventrata as an indoor plant with ornamental foliage and a suitable hanging-basket use. Its climbing/tendril habit supports that placement; the source does not establish a required trellis, mature dimensions or a Garden machine fit.
